subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What percentage of a Muslim's surplus wealth is normally given as zakah?
questions.explain: Zakah is calculated at 2.5% (one-fortieth) of qualifying savings and wealth held for a lunar year.

questions.q: Zakah is best described as which of the following?
options: One of the Five Pillars of Islam
A voluntary act with no set rules
A festival celebrated after Ramadan
A pilgrimage to Makkah
questions.explain: Zakah is the obligatory almsgiving that forms one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

questions.q: What does the term 'nisab' refer to?
options: The minimum amount of wealth a person must own before zakah is due
The name of the Eid charity
The prayer said before giving charity
The list of people who may receive zakah
questions.explain: Nisab is the threshold of wealth below which a Muslim is not required to pay zakah.

options: Voluntary charity given beyond what is obligatory
The fixed 2.5% tax on wealth
The Muslim call to prayer
The pilgrimage rite in Makkah
questions.explain: Sadaqah is voluntary giving offered freely, in contrast to the compulsory zakah.

questions.q: When is zakat al-fitr traditionally given?
options: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer at the end of Ramadan
During the Hajj pilgrimage
On the first day of the new lunar year
Only when a person becomes an adult
questions.explain: Zakat al-fitr is a charitable payment made at the close of Ramadan, before the Eid prayer, so the poor can also celebrate.

questions.q: In which year was the charity Islamic Relief founded in Birmingham?
questions.explain: Islamic Relief was established in Birmingham in 1984 and has since become a major international aid organisation.

questions.q: What does the Arabic term 'ummah' mean?
options: The worldwide community of Muslims
The obligatory charity payment
The Muslim place of worship
The daily prayers
questions.explain: The ummah is the global brotherhood and sisterhood of all Muslims, underpinning ideas of shared social responsibility.

questions.q: Why is giving zakah said to benefit the giver spiritually?
options: It purifies the giver's remaining wealth and reduces greed
It guarantees wealth will double each year
It removes the need to perform daily prayers
It exempts the giver from fasting
questions.explain: Zakah is understood as 'purification', cleansing wealth of selfishness and reminding Muslims that possessions are a trust from God.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes zakah from sadaqah?
options: Zakah is obligatory and fixed, while sadaqah is voluntary and open-ended
Zakah is voluntary, while sadaqah is compulsory
Both are compulsory pillars of Islam
Both may only be given during Ramadan
questions.explain: Zakah is a required, calculated duty, whereas sadaqah is any freely chosen act of generosity.

questions.q: In Islam, why is caring for the poor considered a matter of justice rather than only kindness?
options: Wealth is seen as a trust from God, and the needy have a rightful share in it
The poor must repay any help they receive
Only rulers are responsible for the poor
Charity earns no reward unless it is public
questions.explain: Muslims teach that the poor have a genuine right to a share of others' wealth, making support a duty of justice.

questions.q: Which group is a primary intended recipient of zakah?
options: The poor and needy
Only close family members of the giver
Wealthy business owners
People travelling on holiday for leisure
questions.explain: The Qur'an lists categories such as the poor and needy among those entitled to receive zakah.

questions.q: How does belief in the ummah encourage Muslim social action?
options: It creates a sense of shared responsibility for fellow believers in need worldwide
It teaches that only local charity matters
It discourages helping non-Muslims entirely
It replaces the need for organised charities
questions.explain: Seeing all Muslims as one community motivates giving and relief work across national borders.

questions.q: What is a typical activity of Muslim charities such as Islamic Relief or Muslim Aid?
options: Providing emergency relief and long-term development in poorer regions
Collecting taxes on behalf of governments
Running commercial banks for profit
Organising Hajj travel exclusively
questions.explain: Muslim aid organisations deliver disaster relief, clean water, healthcare and development projects internationally.

questions.q: Which teaching best supports the Muslim emphasis on justice for others?
options: Standing up for fairness and defending the oppressed is a religious duty
Justice applies only to fellow tribe members
Wealth should never be shared with strangers
Helping others cancels the duty of prayer
questions.explain: Islam stresses acting justly and protecting the weak and oppressed as an expression of faith.

questions.q: A Muslim has £2,000 in qualifying savings held for a full lunar year. How much zakah is normally due?
A Muslim wants to give extra money to a local food bank on top of paying zakah. Which term best describes this additional giving?
options: Sadaqah
Zakah
Nisab
Zakat al-fitr
questions.explain: Voluntary giving beyond the obligatory zakah is called sadaqah.

questions.q: After an earthquake overseas, a Muslim family wants to help survivors quickly and reliably. Which action best reflects organised Muslim social action?
options: Donating to an established Muslim aid charity running the relief effort
Waiting until next Ramadan to consider giving
Keeping the money because the victims are far away
Only helping if the victims repay the money later
questions.explain: Supporting recognised charities enables effective, coordinated emergency relief consistent with Muslim social action.

questions.q: A student notices a classmate being treated unfairly. Which response best reflects the Islamic principle of justice and care for others?
options: Speak up and support the classmate against the unfair treatment
Ignore it because it is not their concern
Join in with the unfair treatment
Wait to see if an adult intervenes first
questions.explain: Islam teaches active concern for fairness and standing with those who are wronged.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Religious Studies (0490) syllabus; Islam: Religion & Social Action
